rv.q: But taking the play out of its time is precisely the wrong way to make a case for its timeliness.
The result is slick, moralizing legal pulp, sans drama or philosophical depth.
But in execution, it's more like a rote rehash of familiar material that demands zero thought from its audience.
This is typical of the show, which is adequately done but bland.

Under Ethan McSweeny's conscientious direction, what we get instead is 2-1/ 2 hours of competent acting and monotonous storytelling that seldom elevate the serious plot -- a black man shoots the white men who raped his 10-year-old daughter -- from the genre of theatrical hokum.
These players ensure that the crowd-pleasing A Time to Kill is more than justly served.

James Noone's versatile set, utilizing a tall wood-planked wall and a turntable floor, smoothly glides to multiple locations. Jeff Croiter's lights, Jeff Sugg's projections and Lindsay Jones' sound establish the outside world with visual and audible evidence of Klan rallies, protests and a child's-eye view of the event that sets the story in motion.

While practically none of the performances are deep or nuanced, the cast conveys a sense of urgency that helps make this courtroom drama into the cheesy but crowd-pleasing vehicle that it was intended to be.

Somehow Grisham’s page-turner, which flourished as a film, falls rather flat as a play despite the noisy effects, in Rupert Holmes adaptation staged at the Golden Theater on 45th…not bad, just drawn that way.
All that's missing is the sonic cha-ching between scenes.

Too bad that huge cast doesn’t have a vintage story to tell, because when you strip Grisham’s panoramic tale of racism and injustice in a small Mississippi city down to a courtroom drama, there really isn’t much of a trial at the heart of it.
That cross is one of the few things not half-baked in this production.
But this production has all the snap of a plate of overcooked linguine.
Charged with the dramatic felony of telling instead of showing, "A Time to Kill" is guilty.
Tickets at the box office start at $70.

cn.t: Grisham's courtroom drama receives a mixed-to-negative reception, with critics finding the adaptation formulaic, dated, and lacking dramatic tension. Strong ensemble acting can't overcome one-dimensional characters and plodding pacing.
